1: This briefing comes from Book 01 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, The Transformation Arc.
It's about the move from a domain-joined client-server estate to cloud identity, cloud device management and governed hybrid operations.
Book 01 is the workbook's overview: each part of it points to the book that carries the detail, so think of it as the map.
We'll take four questions: why modernization is so hard, what actually has to change, who leads it, and how to get there.
And if you remember one thing, make it this: modernization is a governance rebuild, not a platform swap.
Let's start with how the estate got here.
2: Because the estate was built in four eras, and each one solved a real problem without keeping what the first era had: one authoritative answer.
On the mainframe, one machine held the data and controlled access to it.
By the late 1980s, that truth was spread across a dozen regional databases and directories.
Then the direction reversed, and data center consolidation wired offices back to distant facilities; the slide has O M B's numbers.
Finally, email and collaboration moved to the cloud, while identity stayed behind in regional domains.
And each fix assumes the last one is finished.
Zero Trust assumes governed identity, governed identity assumes a clean directory, and a clean directory assumes someone owns it.
3: Trust used to come from a session.
In Active Directory, you sign in once and get a Kerberos ticket that lasts ten hours by default.
An account disabled during the day can keep using tickets it got earlier.
Zero Trust decides every request against current policy.

An Entra access token lasts an hour by default, or up to 28 hours with continuous access evaluation, because the service listens for events like a disabled account and stops honoring the token in near real time.
Think of it as a badge checked at every door.
And distance doesn't break tickets, but it does slow every trip to a domain controller.
On the book's arithmetic, Portland to Washington can't beat about 45 milliseconds round trip, whatever the bandwidth.
4: Active Directory was the governance model for every Windows-era service, and nobody wrote it down.
Organizational units exist to apply Group Policy and delegate authority, and both inherit down the tree.

So placing one user in an organizational unit (O U) did five things at once: it chose their administrators, applied every policy along the path, fed the groups built from position, set delegation, and drew an audit boundary.
Entra ID has no O U tree.
Dynamic groups follow attributes, and administrative units scope roles but can't be nested.
Neither rebuilds the tree on its own; that has to be written down on purpose.
And Microsoft still supports Active Directory, so retiring it is the agency's decision, not a vendor deadline.
5: Most A D-to-Entra projects are scoped around users, groups and mailboxes: the visible part.
But the program counts eleven categories of object that Active Directory governs, from service accounts and Group Policy to D N S, certificates, radius and trusts.
Migrate the users, declare victory, and the rest gets left behind.
A certificate doesn't renew, because enrollment was never re-pointed.
A device can't get on the network, because a group lookup comes back empty.
An el-dap application stops, because its bind account was deleted with the domain.

Projects fail because nobody treats five steps as a discipline: enumerate everything, map each dependency to a target, keep delegation continuous, deliver through a governed pipeline, and watch for drift.
6: Before anything moves, the program needs one place where every decision is written down, signed and replayable.
Chapter 03 describes a reference host for that: one Windows Server 2025 server, with a standby.
It carries five roles, from a version-controlled source of truth with signed commits to an adapter for each dependency category; the slide lists them all.
What matters most is that there's a single authoritative writer.
And governance and execution never mix.
One layer validates and signs plans, but never touches a target.
The other runs authorized plans, but decides nothing, with separate accounts, credentials and logs.
The host reads Active Directory read-only, and it's protected as Tier 0.
7: Identity comes first, because every later control reads its attributes.
For the workforce, the authoritative source is the HR system of record.

Four mechanisms rebuild what the O U tree did: attributes replace O U placement, dynamic groups replace O U-based groups, administrative units replace O U delegation, and Conditional Access replaces Group Policy inheritance.
The program's contribution is what ties them together: one HR-sourced stamp drives membership, delegation, policy targeting, licensing and drift detection.
Dynamic membership usually updates within a few hours, but it can take more than a day, so design job moves around that delay.
And HR provisioning must be the only thing that writes those attributes.
Books 02 and 03 carry identity in depth.
8: Group Policy was Active Directory's most ambitious delivery system, and its most network-bound.
A client only gets it when it can reach a domain controller.
A cloud-native device, Entra joined and in Intune, has no such dependency.
A fifty-setting G P O ported as fifty settings carries dead weight, old conflicts and manual targeting, and Microsoft itself recommends starting fresh.

So the program regenerates one clean policy per category, keyed to attributes, into Intune, Conditional Access and, for servers, Azure machine configuration, because Intune doesn't manage Windows Server.
Every change passes four stages: validation, a simulated tenant, a report-only pilot, then production.
And prefer require over block, except where the federal scuba baseline demands a block.
9: D N S, DHCP and address management are what agencies most often put off, because they still work.
That's exactly how they keep the old directory alive.
A D-integrated zones replicate with Active Directory, and domain-joined clients find their domain controllers through records in D N S, so D N S and A D have to be retired together, in sequence.
The target is a governed D N S authority outside A D. Windows DHCP servers check in with A D every hour, but that only stops a rogue Windows server, not a rogue device.
And one address-management authority owns the address space, with D N S and DHCP following from it.
Leave these three for “Phase 2,” and it rarely comes.
A forest that still hosts D N S hasn't been retired.
10: Once identity, policy and services have moved, the biggest remaining dependency is the domain join itself.
User PCs end up Entra joined and in Intune.
Servers come under Azure Arc and machine configuration.
Hybrid join is a waypoint, not a destination.
And there's no supported way to convert a hybrid-joined device without resetting Windows, so time the move to a hardware refresh.
Every service principal name is an application that expects Kerberos, and each needs a decision: move it to modern authentication, retire it, or, as a last resort, isolate it with an end date.
No server leaves the domain until every one is resolved, and N T L M goes in the same pass.
And compute stays with its data until the round trips are cut down.
11: When Active Directory retires, being inside the network stops meaning anything.
M twenty-two oh-nine puts it simply: users should log into applications, not networks.
The replacement has four parts: Zero Trust as the model, Conditional Access as the per-request decision, sassy at the edge, and phishing-resistant M F A as the proof.
B O D twenty-five oh-one makes blocking legacy authentication mandatory.
Entra certificate-based authentication moves card validation from the domain controller to Entra ID, though a card only counts as phishing-resistant if it's set up as multifactor.
And card issuance needs a successor first, because an enterprise CA depends on A D. Administrators hold no standing privilege: roles are activated just in time, and a vault covers what can't be.
Book 04 covers policy and privilege, and Book 07 the certificates.
12: Chapter 09 sums it up in one line: Microsoft provides the instruments; the program provides the orchestra.
The tools are each excellent, but none of them decides what the organization's structure should become, or what to do with what they find, and no vendor deadline forces that decision.
So name one decider for each kind of decision.
The sponsor and C I O own scope, funding, sequence, and when A D components retire.
The authorizing official is the only one who can accept risk, so every deferred cutoff lands with them.
The see-so sets control requirements, and the steward holds the repository and clears most gates.
Then, each month, ask three things: how drift is trending, whether changes are signed, and what risk acceptances are open.
13: You can't modernize what you haven't counted, and nothing gets retired until it's written down: read-only, with proof of how it was read.
The assessment account has no write rights, the code can't issue write commands, and every call is logged.
An ordinary signed-in account already sees more than most teams expect: the topology, the O U tree, most Group Policy, users and groups.
Every run records who, when, against what, and a hash of every file.
Eleven streams feed the risk scoring.
One example: Windows Server 2016 reaches end of support on January 12, 2027, so every such server needs a disposition.
And no application leaves its data until its transactions are profiled.
14: Chapter 11 turns the inventory into change, in three stages.
Analyze compares the current state with the target and produces a diff.
Plan expands that diff into actions, each scoped to one object, put in dependency order, and paired with its rollback.
A plan has to pass validation, then approval by someone who didn't write it.
Then a separate identity carries it out and closes with an evidence packet.
How far automation may go is capped by a ladder, from simply recording, up to autonomy for a short list of low-risk changes.
The default ceiling is gated actuation, because it's a posture an authorizing official can sign.
sis-uh calls its maturity model a general guide, not a strict set of requirements, so this is design, not mandate.
And when nothing has drifted, the next run plans zero actions.
15: Chapter 12 puts it all in sequence: an illustrative fifty-two-week program, seven phases from pre-flight to steady state, with five workstreams in parallel.
Large federal estates usually take several years; the weeks are a sequencing model, not a promise.
A phase opens only when the previous gate clears, and gates read from data.
“Zero drift for fourteen days” is a query, not a signature.
Underneath it all is one structural move: separate truth from enforcement.
A governance layer holds and reconciles the authoritative state, while the identity, network and device platforms enforce it at runtime.
And read one clock carefully: fed-ramp's 2027 date is about certifying cloud providers.
The agency still authorizes its own systems.
That brings us to the decisions.
16: First, name the owners, one decider per decision, starting with the sponsor, the authorizing official and the steward, and confirm who holds the Zero Trust lead role that M twenty-two oh-nine required.
Second, run the read-only assessment across all eleven categories, with provenance.
Third, stand up the platform host, so every change has one writer and a plan.
And fourth, set the dates: gate dates on the sponsor's calendar, and every exception's end date on the authorizing official's.
None of this needs a vendor decision on day one.
Start with an inventory, an owner, and a date.
Modernization is a governance rebuild, not a platform swap.
Book 01 is the map, and Books 02 to 09 carry each part in depth, with every claim footnoted.
